# Results — Study 1026 (Gibson's Paradox) on the real tapes

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py) in 14 s. Every
series is read from tapes frozen inside the `arch` and `statsmodels` wheels through
[`quantlab/bundled.py`](../../../quantlab/bundled.py) — no network. As-of **2018-11-30** (the
last full month common to the AAA, core-CPI and T-bill tapes). Yields are **nominal**, percent;
prices are 100 × log index; the macro tapes are **final-vintage**.*

**The limit that frames everything.** Gibson's paradox is a gold-standard regularity. These tapes
carry Moody's yields back to 1919 but **no price index before 1957**, so the era in which the
paradox is supposed to live cannot be tested here. This is a test of the investor's version under
**fiat money**: 1957-2018 in the US, 1972-98 in Germany.

## 1. Levels — what the claim is built on (descriptive, not evidence)

Correlation of the long yield with each price variable.

| Tape | Period | Raw log price | Price gap (expanding) | Price gap (rolling 10y) | Inflation | Adaptive exp. (36m) |
|---|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| US monthly | 1957-2018 | -0.00 | **+0.80** | +0.03 | +0.75 | +0.91 |
| US monthly | 1965-81 | +0.92 | **+0.95** | +0.50 | +0.86 | +0.94 |
| US monthly | 1982-2018 | -0.96 | **+0.96** | -0.46 | +0.87 | +0.96 |
| US quarterly (headline) | 1959-2009 | +0.23 | **+0.67** | -0.09 | +0.59 | n/a |
| Germany | 1972-98 | -0.58 | **+0.44** | +0.44 | +0.70 | n/a |

The raw price level is a clock under fiat money: it correlates +0.92 with
the AAA yield in 1965-81, when both rose, and -0.96 in 1982-2018, when prices
kept rising and yields fell. Detrended past-only from the start of the sample, the gap tracks
yields at +0.80 — higher than 12-month inflation (+0.75). That is the
paradox in its modern dress. Section 2 is why none of these numbers is evidence.

## 2. Unit roots — the spurious-regression trap

ADF (H0: unit root) and KPSS (H0: stationary), constant only.

| Series | n | ADF p | KPSS p | Reading |
|---|--:|--:|--:|---|
| US AAA yield | 743 | 0.548 | 0.010 | **I(1)-like** |
| US ΔAAA | 742 | 0.000 | 0.100 | not I(1)-like |
| US log core CPI | 743 | 0.594 | 0.010 | **I(1)-like** |
| US 1m inflation (Δlog CPI) | 742 | 0.078 | 0.010 | **I(1)-like** |
| US 12m inflation | 731 | 0.056 | 0.010 | **I(1)-like** |
| US price gap (expanding) | 684 | 0.932 | 0.010 | **I(1)-like** |
| US price gap (rolling 10y) | 624 | 0.008 | 0.010 | not I(1)-like |
| US adaptive exp. (36m) | 742 | 0.566 | 0.010 | **I(1)-like** |
| DE long rate | 107 | 0.327 | 0.010 | **I(1)-like** |
| DE 4q inflation | 104 | 0.561 | 0.010 | **I(1)-like** |
| DE price gap (expanding) | 85 | 0.154 | 0.070 | not I(1)-like |

The yield, the log price level, inflation and the expanding price gap all read as I(1)-like.
Correlating levels of such series is exactly the Granger-Newbold (1974) trap: two independent
random walks routinely correlate at ±0.5 with t-statistics in the dozens.

## 3. Cointegration — is there a long-run relation at all?

Engle-Granger (H0: no cointegration) of the yield on each variable. The "naive t" is the levels-
OLS t-statistic the trap produces; read it as a warning, not a result.

| Tape | Yield on… | Naive levels t | R² | EG p |
|---|---|--:|--:|--:|
| US monthly | log price level (raw) | -0.1 | 0.00 | **0.770** |
| US monthly | price gap (expanding) | +36.8 | 0.65 | **0.194** |
| US monthly | price gap (rolling 10y) | +0.6 | 0.00 | **0.839** |
| US monthly | 12m inflation | +24.4 | 0.56 | **0.275** |
| US monthly | adaptive expectation (36m) | +61.4 | 0.83 | **0.009** |
| Germany | price gap (expanding) | +4.2 | 0.20 | **0.377** |
| Germany | 4q inflation | +12.9 | 0.49 | **0.087** |

The yield is **not** cointegrated with the price gap (p = 0.19) nor with 12-month
inflation (p = 0.28) — despite naive t-statistics in the dozens. It **is**
cointegrated with an adaptive inflation expectation (p = 0.009); see §5.

## 4. First differences — the horse race (Newey-West)

ΔY on Δgap and Δπ jointly; the last two columns are each alone. In differences, Gibson's claim
reads "yield changes follow the price change (= inflation)", Fisher's "yield changes follow the
change in inflation".

| Tape | Period | n | b gap | **t gap** | b infl. | **t infl.** | t gap alone | t infl. alone |
|---|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| US monthly AAA | 1957-2018 | 683 | +0.231 | **+3.56** | +0.028 | **+0.38** | +4.25 | +2.55 |
| US monthly AAA | 1965-81 | 204 | +0.221 | **+2.37** | +0.006 | **+0.06** | +2.48 | +1.65 |
| US monthly AAA | 1982-2018 | 443 | +0.184 | **+1.59** | +0.124 | **+1.27** | +2.36 | +2.19 |
| US monthly BAA | 1957-2018 | 683 | +0.328 | **+4.00** | -0.009 | **-0.17** | +5.78 | +4.37 |
| US quarterly (headline) | 1959-2009 | 183 | +0.311 | **+3.66** | +0.021 | **+0.36** | +4.76 | +3.85 |
| Germany | 1972-98 | 84 | +0.016 | **+0.07** | -0.126 | **-1.00** | -0.43 | -1.13 |

On the US tape the gap wins: t = +3.56 against +0.38 for inflation in the
joint regression, and it holds on headline CPI (macrodata) and for BAA yields. Germany shows
nothing either way. The regime split is not significant: gap slope 1982-2018 minus 1965-81 =
-0.038 (HAC t -0.25).

## 5. The confound — Fisher with a long memory

Fisher (1930) explained Gibson's correlation with **slowly adapting inflation expectations**: if
expected inflation is a long distributed lag of past inflation, the yield tracks a smoothed
*cumulation* of inflation, which is what a detrended price level is. Proxy: an exponentially
weighted average of one-month inflation (past-only). The whole half-life grid is shown, not a
chosen point; the headline uses 36 months, the middle of it.

| Half-life (months) | Corr with yield (levels) | EG p | Corr(Δgap, Δexp.) | t gap (joint Δ) | t exp. (joint Δ) |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 12 | +0.84 | **0.151** | 0.90 | +1.71 | +0.03 |
| 36 | +0.91 | **0.009** | 0.98 | +1.28 | +0.04 |
| 60 | +0.91 | **0.008** | 0.97 | +1.53 | +0.08 |
| 120 | +0.86 | **0.077** | 0.92 | +1.58 | +0.09 |

In changes the gap and the adaptive expectation are nearly the same variable (correlation
≥ 0.9), so the difference regression cannot separate them — the gap's t drops to
+1.28. In levels the adaptive expectation fits the yield better than the gap
*and* is cointegrated with it, which the gap is not. The US "Gibson" signal is most economically
read as **Fisher with a long memory**, which is the resolution Fisher himself proposed.

## 6. Out of sample — does the price level tell you where yields go?

Expanding window, minimum 120 months (Germany 40 quarters) of realised
outcomes; the price variable is lagged one period for CPI publication. Benchmark = yield-level-
only model (mean reversion); Clark-West (2007) one-sided test of the improvement.

| Tape | Horizon | Added variable | n | First forecast | OOS R² vs yield-only | CW t | CW p |
|---|---|---|--:|---|--:|--:|--:|
| US monthly | 3m | price gap (expanding) | 558 | 1972-03-31 | +0.014 | +3.79 | **0.000** |
| US monthly | 3m | price gap (rolling 10y) | 498 | 1977-03-31 | -0.009 | +0.59 | **0.276** |
| US monthly | 3m | 12m / 4q inflation | 605 | 1968-04-30 | +0.032 | +2.17 | **0.015** |
| US monthly | 3m | adaptive exp. (36m) | 616 | 1967-05-31 | +0.036 | +4.21 | **0.000** |
| US monthly | 12m | price gap (expanding) | 540 | 1972-12-31 | +0.035 | +4.45 | **0.000** |
| US monthly | 12m | price gap (rolling 10y) | 480 | 1977-12-31 | -0.092 | -0.92 | **0.821** |
| US monthly | 12m | 12m / 4q inflation | 587 | 1969-01-31 | +0.069 | +2.28 | **0.011** |
| US monthly | 12m | adaptive exp. (36m) | 598 | 1968-02-29 | +0.086 | +3.68 | **0.000** |
| Germany | 1q | price gap (expanding) | 43 | 1988-03-31 | -0.365 | -1.78 | **0.963** |
| Germany | 1q | 12m / 4q inflation | 62 | 1983-06-30 | -0.023 | -0.11 | **0.545** |
| Germany | 4q | price gap (expanding) | 37 | 1988-12-31 | -0.823 | -1.27 | **0.898** |
| Germany | 4q | 12m / 4q inflation | 56 | 1984-03-31 | -0.089 | -0.04 | **0.516** |

The expanding gap improves the US forecast at both horizons; the rolling-window gap — the same
idea, detrended over ten years instead of the whole history — does not (p = 0.82).
Germany's samples are short (≈ 40-60 forecasts) and show nothing.

## 7. Could you trade it? A duration overlay on a 20-year AAA par bond

**Bond return (the duration approximation, stated):** r[t+1] ≈ Y[t]/12 − D[t]·ΔY + ½·C[t]·ΔY²,
D and C the modified duration and convexity of a 20-year semi-annual par bond at the Moody's AAA
yield (mean D ≈ 11.0). Excess of the one-month T-bill (Fama-French RF).
**Rule:** at each month-end, 1.5× duration if the 12-month forecast of the yield change is below
the prevailing mean change, else 0.5×; the weight set at *t* earns month *t+1* (one execution lag),
CPI lagged one month on top. Costs 5 bp one-way × NAV traded. Benchmark:
constant 1× duration. All Sharpe ratios are **excess-of-cash vs excess-of-cash**.

| Timer (12m forecast) | Gross Sharpe | Net Sharpe | Constant Sharpe | Net − constant /yr | HAC t | Mean position | Turnover /yr | Alpha vs constant (t) | By regime (net − constant) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|---|
| price gap (expanding) | 0.54 | 0.54 | 0.50 | **+1.95%** | +2.63 | 1.43 | 0.13 | +0.65% (+1.01) | 1965-81 -0.05% (t -0.0) · 1982-2018 +2.44% (t +3.2) |
| price gap (rolling 10y) | 0.32 | 0.32 | 0.54 | **-1.92%** | -2.46 | 0.78 | 0.12 | -1.22% (-1.40) | 1965-81 -4.15% (t -2.1) · 1982-2018 -1.68% (t -2.0) |
| 12m inflation | 0.54 | 0.54 | 0.48 | **+1.08%** | +1.47 | 1.10 | 0.40 | +0.94% (+1.37) | 1965-81 -0.53% (t -0.4) · 1982-2018 +1.64% (t +2.0) |
| adaptive exp. (36m) | 0.51 | 0.51 | 0.46 | **+1.05%** | +1.46 | 1.16 | 0.57 | +0.78% (+1.18) | 1965-81 -0.18% (t -0.1) · 1982-2018 +1.51% (t +1.9) |
| yield level only | 0.37 | 0.37 | 0.50 | **-1.27%** | -1.64 | 0.86 | 0.11 | -0.51% (-0.63) | 1965-81 -1.01% (t -0.5) · 1982-2018 -1.33% (t -1.6) |

Cost sweep for the gap timer:

| One-way cost (bp) | Net − constant /yr | HAC t | Net Sharpe |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 | +1.96% | +2.63 | 0.54 |
| 2 | +1.96% | +2.63 | 0.54 |
| 5 | +1.95% | +2.63 | 0.54 |
| 10 | +1.95% | +2.62 | 0.54 |
| 25 | +1.93% | +2.59 | 0.54 |
| 50 | +1.89% | +2.54 | 0.54 |

The gap timer beats constant duration by +1.95% a year (t
+2.63) and the yield-only timer by +3.22% (t
+3.32). It trades 0.13× NAV a year, so costs are
irrelevant (break-even 1499 bp). What it is: a near-static long-duration call
held through the 1982-2018 bond bull, with nothing to show in 1965-81 — one regime, one trade.

## 8. Synthetic control — can the machinery tell the worlds apart?

Same price path; the yield is a Fisher world (s = 0), a Gibson world (s = 1) or an even blend.
A **machinery proof only** — never evidence about markets.

| signal_strength | Gibson legs (L1 coint · L2 Δ · L3 OOS) | Fisher legs | t gap | t infl. | EG p gap | EG p infl. |
|--:|---|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0.0 | L1 ✘ · L2 ✘ · L3 ✘ | L1 ✔ · L2 ✔ · L3 ✘ | +0.80 | +10.21 | 0.453 | 0.000 |
| 0.5 | L1 ✘ · L2 ✔ · L3 ✘ | L1 ✘ · L2 ✔ · L3 ✔ | +2.60 | +4.49 | 0.060 | 0.087 |
| 1.0 | L1 ✔ · L2 ✔ · L3 ✔ | L1 ✘ · L2 ✘ · L3 ✔ | +4.40 | -1.23 | 0.000 | 0.698 |

## Caveats

- **No gold standard.** No price index before 1957 on these tapes; the paradox's home era is
  untested. A fiat-era answer is not an answer about 1820-1913.
- **Moody's AAA is a seasoned corporate index**, not a Treasury: it carries a credit spread and an
  average maturity of 20+ years that drifts. The par-bond return is an approximation, not an
  investable index's total return; there is no long AAA futures contract, so the overlay would be
  run with Treasury futures and carry basis risk.
- **Final-vintage macro.** Core CPI is barely revised and is lagged one month here; the German
  deflator and the macrodata CPI are revised series.
- **The price gap is a choice.** Expanding-from-1957 detrending works, rolling 10-year does not.
  A different start date would move the expanding trend too; the result is specification-
  sensitive and the desk says so on the Signal axis.
- **Clark-West with overlapping 12-month targets** uses Newey-West with h + 2 lags; the timer's
  t-statistics use 12 lags on monthly P&L.
- **Germany is short** (107 quarters, ≈ 40-60 out-of-sample forecasts): low power, but also no
  hint of the effect at all.

## Verdict

Produced by `strategy.verdict` (rules in `signal_stamp` / `trad_stamp`), fixed before the run
and unit-tested in [`tests/test_strategy.py`](../tests/test_strategy.py).

**Signal: Mixed.** Split by tape. **US (core CPI, 1957-2018): the price gap wins the horse race against 12-month inflation.** In first differences, with both in the regression, the gap's Newey-West t is **+3.56** and inflation's **+0.38**; out of sample the (publication-lagged) gap improves a yield-only forecast of the next year's yield change at Clark-West p = 0.000 (inflation p = 0.011). US Gibson legs passed: L2, L3. **Germany (1972-98): nothing** — gap t +0.07, inflation t -1.00, legs passed: none. Three things keep this from Real. (1) *No cointegration*: the yield and the price gap do not share a stochastic trend (Engle-Granger p = 0.19), so the famous level correlation (+0.80 with the gap; the raw log price level flips from +0.92 in 1965-81 to -0.96 in 1982-2018) is two trends, not a law. (2) *Fisher with a long memory explains it better*: an adaptive inflation expectation (exponential average, 36-month half-life) correlates +0.91 with the yield and **is** cointegrated with it (p = 0.009); in differences the two are near-identical and the gap's edge over it shrinks to t +1.28 — Irving Fisher's own 1930 resolution of the paradox, visible on a modern tape. (3) *Specification*: detrend the price level over a rolling 10-year window instead of the full history and the out-of-sample edge disappears (Clark-West p = 0.82). The tapes hold no price index before 1957, so the gold-standard paradox itself is untested here.

**Tradability: Fragile.** As a duration overlay on a 20-year AAA par bond (1.5× duration when the expanding-window forecast of next year's yield change is below its prevailing mean, else 0.5×; CPI lagged a month, one execution lag, 5 bp one-way), the gap timer earned **+1.95% a year net over constant duration (HAC t +2.63)** with net excess Sharpe 0.54 vs 0.50. But it trades 0.13× NAV a year and sat at 1.43× duration on average — it is essentially one regime call, long duration through the 1982-2018 bond bull; by regime: 1965-81 -0.05% (t -0.0); 1982-2018 +2.44% (t +3.2). Its alpha after regressing on constant duration is +0.65% (t +1.01). It beats a yield-only timer (+3.22% a year). Costs are not the problem (break-even 1499 bp); one secular trade and zero in the Great Inflation is.

> **In one sentence:** Under fiat money Gibson's paradox survives only as a shadow of Fisher: the detrended price level beats 12-month inflation on the US tape but not in Germany, and it is not cointegrated with yields while long-memory inflation expectations are; the duration timer it implies earns +1.95% a year net (t +2.6) from what is really one long bet on the 1982-2018 bond bull.
